items.title: 68113_Barney Bigard oral history interview
items.q: all these supposed to be big-time clarinetists like Picou, he showed me where they wasn't nothing.

ctx.x: What musicians did you work with?

I worked with Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly. I worked with Manuel Perez. I had an opportunity to work with him. And I worked with Piron. Another fantastic trumpet man that nobody don't hear anything about is Amos White, and he's a professor at Berklee College of Music -- in music, a very fantastic man. He taught me a lot. And we had a band together and he took me around, and all these supposed to be big-time clarinetists like Picou, he showed me where they wasn't nothing. He did, too. Because he liked me and he was…
I had a wonderful time, but I left. I was known as the "Slap Tongue King."

items.title: Barney Bigard Interview, Early 1970s
items.q: I copied anybody I could. Anybody? I used to, I loved Jimmy Noon, and I loved Big I, Louis, and of course I loved my teacher Lorenzo Teo, and I loved Alphonse Piku

ctx.x: Who were some of the people that you were copying at the time? Who, me? Yeah.

I copied anybody I could. Anybody? I used to, I loved Jimmy Noon, and I loved Big I, Louis, and of course I loved my teacher Lorenzo Teo, and I loved Alphonse Piku, and they were about the best, as far as the clarinet is concerned, they were about the best down there.
This was really the experimental, the pioneering stage of music, wasn't it, where no one had been, shall we say, moving in the direction of this kind of music, and these were fellas that were-
